body: This naturally lead to the second research question of the thesis concerning how the Arctic security strategies and foreign policies of Russia and the United States can impact the geopolitical climate in the Arctic region at large, the analysis again point to that the threat perception of the Other plays a crucial part in answering this question. The analysis shows from a conventional constructive perspective that both Russia and the United States perceive the Other part to act in a threatful manner, and that this process, in which the Other is given the identity of an enemy, has the potential to impact the overall geopolitical Arctic climate the most. This due to the fact that, just as previous research has shown, both Russia and the United States aspire to cooperate with other Arctic states that they have no threat perception of, while simultaneously being highly hesitant towards cooperating with each other. The United States in particular is very vocal about its Russian threat perception, while Russia only addresses the United States as an enemy directly regarding its maritime policies, whilst being more discrete in its Arctic policies. This might be related to the fact that Russia tries to balance international cooperation with its security needs, in addition to the fact that Russia economically benefits from the Arctic being a peaceful and cooperative region (Lagutina 2021: 118; Staun 2023: 5).

The relationship between the two Arctic superpowers can also be explained with conventional constructivism in the sense that both Russia and the United States in their Arctic policies are forced to “mirror back the representation it has contributed to the other” (Wendt 1999: 263), but also further exposes the lack of a central authority and the Arctic governance vacuum that previous research has accounted for (Staun & Sørensen 2023: 36).
